readerTitle: The one-hour meeting that costs twelve hours
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식당 주간 회의, 소프트웨어 스타트업 데일리 스탠드업) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 회의 시간은 '1시간'이 아니라 '참석자 수 × 시간'이다. 그래서 회의는 먼저 결과(정할 것)를 정하고, 그 결과에 필요한 사람만 부른다.
misconception: 회의를 짧게 줄이면 회의 비용 문제는 해결된다. 모두가 참석해야 공정하고 정보가 잘 퍼진다.

sources.text: 회의 운영의 일반 원칙 (목적 정의, 참석자 선정, 결정·담당자·기한 정리)

factChecks.note: 스탠드업: 10명 × 45분 = 450분 = 7.5인시/일, × 주 5일 = 37.5인시/주 (풀타임 1명 근무시간에 가까움). 시급 가정 없이 시간으로만 표기.

cards.title: The one-hour meeting that costs twelve hours
body: Every Monday at 3 p.m., a restaurant owner gathers all 12 staff for an hour. Sales updates, the rota, a new supplier, and then the new autumn menu.
On the calendar it's one hour. On the payroll it's twelve.

image.label: Twelve staff around restaurant tables, each with a small clock
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 영업 전 식당, 테이블을 붙여 12명의 직원(셰프, 서버, 바텐더)이 둘러앉음. 각 사람 머리 위에 작은 1시간짜리 시계. 벽시계는 3시. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: How would you cut the cost of Monday's meeting?
body: Most of the hour is updates. Only one item needs a real decision: how to roll out the new menu. Four people decide that: the owner, the head chef, the floor manager and the bar lead.
What change saves the most staff time without losing anything important?

options.text: Keep everyone, but cut the meeting to 30 minutes
options.feedback: It halves the cost, but the menu decision gets squeezed into a rushed slot with eight people who don't need to be there.

options.text: Send updates in a short written note, then meet 20 minutes with only the four people deciding the menu
options.feedback: Everyone still gets the news, and the decision gets focused time. It trades a shared moment for about 80% of the hours back. Next card shows the math.

options.text: Keep the hour, but send an agenda the day before
options.feedback: An agenda helps people prepare, but twelve people still spend an hour on items that mostly involve four of them.

cards.title: Count people, not minutes.
body: Assume staff earn about $20 an hour. The written note takes each person about 5 minutes to read. The new setup costs around **$47 a week** instead of $240.
cards.callout: Shortening a meeting cuts minutes. Choosing who attends cuts hours.

cards.title: Running a meeting starts before it begins
body: A meeting spends the time of everyone in the room at once. So **running meetings** well means deciding, before anyone sits down, what the meeting must produce.

Most meetings do one of three jobs: share information, make a decision, or solve a problem together. Sharing information rarely needs everyone in a room. Decisions and problem-solving do, but only with the people who can contribute or must act.

image.label: Three doors labeled Inform, Decide, Solve
image.brief: 세 개의 문 일러스트. "Inform" 문 앞에는 메모지와 휴대폰 알림, "Decide" 문 앞에는 4개의 의자, "Solve" 문 앞에는 화이트보드. 단순하고 밝은 색감.

cards.title: Four habits of a meeting worth its hours
body: Each habit answers one question about the meeting.
list: **Before:** write the outcome in one sentence. *"We leave with a launch date for the new menu."*
**Invite:** who decides, who knows something needed, who must act on the result. Everyone else gets a note.
**During:** start with the question, not with updates.
**End:** read back each decision, who owns it and by when.
cards.callout: If you can't write the outcome sentence, you may not need the meeting yet.

cards.title: Sometimes the whole team should be there.
body: The same restaurant holds a 10-minute huddle before every dinner service: tonight's specials, dishes that have run out, a big table at eight. All 12 attend.
That's 2 staff-hours a night, and it's worth it. Every person acts on what they hear within minutes. The rule isn't "fewer people." It's that **everyone in the room needs what the meeting produces.**

cards.title: Not every hour in a meeting is wasted.
body: Meetings also build trust, let people be heard and catch problems nobody wrote down. Cut them all and people start working blind.
Written updates only work if people actually read them. Keep notes short and check that they land.
And don't use the cost math to shut out the people who see the problem up close. A server may know why a dish isn't selling.

cards.title: Now it's a software team's daily standup.
body: A startup's 10 engineers and designers meet every morning for a "15-minute" standup. Each person reads out yesterday's work. It usually runs 45 minutes.
That's 7.5 people-hours a day, or 37.5 a week, close to one full-time person. What would you change?

options.text: Post daily updates in a shared written channel, and keep 15 minutes only for blockers, with just the people involved
options.feedback: Updates still flow, and the meeting time goes to problems that need people talking. You trade the ritual of everyone speaking for most of those hours back.
It frees all the hours, but blockers may sit unseen for days. A small daily meeting with a clear job is cheap insurance.

options.text: Keep the format, but use a strict 15-minute timer
options.feedback: It cuts the cost to a third, but ten people still listen to updates they could read in a minute.

cards.title: A meeting costs its length times everyone in it.
body: Decide what the meeting must produce, invite only the people that outcome needs, and end with who does what by when.
**Try it today:** pick your next recurring meeting. Multiply attendees by its length, then write its outcome in one sentence.
